title: I’m feeling more optimistic about American politics
gist: After the Democrats' midterm blue wave, Noah Smith turns more optimistic on US politics because liberals and moderates, not the DSA-style hard left, led the win; voters simultaneously backed centrist/right-leaning ballot measures (tax caps, voter ID); and leaders are starting to tackle anti-development policy. The captured text cuts off at a paywall mid-way through the second of his three trends (the corruption section is not included).

themes.theme: Midterm blue wave reshapes the parties

insights.claim: Noah Smith says the midterm elections punished the Republican Party for going along with Trump's transformation of it, and this underpins his newfound marginal optimism about American politics.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shifts the policy outlook toward a Democrat-influenced Congress; watch for legislative agenda changes in 2027.
insights.quote: it’s refreshing to see America punish the GOP for going along with that transformation
insights.locator: A lot of this is downstream

insights.claim: Smith identifies three positive trends: Democrats are not becoming extremist as fast as he feared, there is real bipartisan movement on good federal policymaking, and the nation is waking up to corruption and holding perpetrators to account.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A framework for tracking whether US policy shifts toward pragmatic, growth-oriented legislation.

insights.claim: Smith still partly entertains his January thesis that liberal democracy suffered a generational failure, so his optimism is marginal rather than a reversal.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Tempers the optimistic read; structural political risk remains in his view.
insights.quote: To be honest, I still entertain that notion.

themes.theme: Liberals, not the DSA left, led the anti-Trump charge

insights.claim: Smith admits he was wrong in August to predict that a Democratic midterm victory would be led by a hard-left DSA vanguard.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Lowers the odds of a sharply left-wing Democratic policy agenda (e.g., radical tax or anti-business measures).
insights.quote: Well, happily, I was wrong about this.

insights.claim: Francesca Hong, a DSA-type candidate expected to be a statewide Democratic nominee, was defeated in the Democratic primary in an upset, showing even partisan Democrats aren't sold on the DSA faction.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Evidence that Democratic primary voters are filtering out hard-left candidates.

insights.claim: Despite the blue wave, most high-profile DSA-faction candidates performed significantly worse than their 'normie' Democrat counterparts, according to data from Jeff Maurer cited by Smith.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Moderate candidates outperform; expect Democratic strategy to tilt centrist for 2028.
insights.quote: most of the high-profile DSA-faction candidates performed significantly worse than their normie Democrat counterparts
insights.locator: Even more importantly, the hard left

insights.claim: Voters who elected Democrats also approved centrist or right-leaning ballot measures: North Carolina approved a 3.5% state income tax cap, a property-tax levy limit and photo ID; Iowa made state income taxes harder to raise; Ohio backed photo ID by two-thirds; Wisconsin banned affirmative action in state institutions.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: State-level tax constraints (income tax caps, property-tax limits) persist even under Democratic wins; relevant for state fiscal outlooks and munis.
insights.quote: The second would cap the state income tax at 3.5 percent

insights.claim: Smith argues the scale of the Democratic victory effectively disempowers the DSA faction in Congress because marginal seats are won by purple-state moderates, keeping moderates like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer in leadership.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Expect moderate congressional leadership and a more predictable, business-tolerable legislative agenda.
insights.locator: And in Congress, the sheer scale

insights.claim: Jon Ossoff's potential as a 2028 presidential contender surged after his large midterm win, while leftist enthusiasm for AOC has dimmed with no obvious left replacement.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Early read on 2028: a mainstream liberal nominee is more likely than a left-populist one.
insights.locator: Note that the knives are already

insights.claim: Smith predicts that if leftists fail to find a 2028 candidate and Democrats retake the White House with a normie liberal, the leftist faction may miss America's 'decade of unrest' entirely, which he considers good for the nation.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Points to reduced tail risk of radical economic policy from a 2029 Democratic administration.
insights.locator: If they fail to find a candidate

insights.claim: Smith senses a 'vibe shift' in which people are less ashamed to support Obama-style early-2010s liberalism and liberal influencers are pushing back more on leftist voices.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Soft cultural signal of a centrist turn in Democratic politics.

themes.theme: Anti-development policy as the core Democratic problem

insights.claim: Smith argues the worst Democratic policy problems are state and local anti-development rules that make housing, roads, trains, power stations and transmission lines prohibitively hard or expensive to build, freezing the built environment in the 1970s.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Permitting/land-use reform is the key unlock for construction, utilities and grid buildout; track reform as a catalyst.
insights.quote: freezing our built environment in the 1970s

insights.claim: Smith sees signs that America's leaders now recognize the anti-development problem and are taking action to fix it, framed as smart policy winning and interest 'groups' starting to lose.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Positive for homebuilders, infrastructure and energy developers if pro-building reforms advance.
insights.quote: Now there are signs that at long last, America’s leaders recognize this problem and are taking action to fix it.
